content: Gypsum is an exceptionally soft mineral that consists of calcium sulfate dihydrate, chemically represented as CaSO₄·2H₂O. In its natural state, gypsum can form as flattened, often twinned crystals or as transparent, cleavable masses known as selenite. It can also appear in a silky, fibrous form, commonly referred to as satin spar. Additionally, gypsum may present as granular or compact masses. When observed in hand-sized samples, its appearance can range from transparent to opaque. A fine-grained, white or lightly tinted variety of gypsum, called alabaster, is highly valued for ornamental purposes. In arid regions, gypsum can crystallize into a flower-like structure, often opaque and embedded with sand grains, known as desert rose. The most visually striking form of gypsum is found in the Naica Mine, where giant crystals, some reaching up to 11 meters in length, have been discovered. Recent studies indicate that these massive crystals formed under stable temperature conditions, allowing for slow and steady growth without excessive nucleation. Gypsum is a widely distributed mineral, often found in thick evaporite beds associated with sedimentary rocks. Deposits of gypsum have been identified in strata dating back to the Permian period. It is deposited in various environments, including lake and seawater, hot springs, volcanic vapors, and sulfate-rich solutions in veins. Hydrothermal anhydrite in veins is frequently hydrated to gypsum by groundwater near the Earth's surface. Gypsum is commonly associated with other minerals such as halite and sulfur. The term gypsum originates from the Greek verb μαγειρεύω (mageiréuō), meaning to cook, referencing the calcined or burnt form of the mineral. Historically, gypsum from the Montmartre district of Paris was extensively used to produce burnt gypsum, known as plaster of Paris. This material has been utilized for various applications, including construction and artistic purposes. Gypsum is also incorporated into products like foot creams, shampoos, and other hair care items. It is water-soluble, and because it dissolves over time in water, it is rarely found in the form of sand. However, the unique conditions at White Sands National Monument in New Mexico have resulted in a vast 710 km² (275 square mile) expanse of white gypsum sand, sufficient to supply the construction industry with drywall for 1,000 years. In 1933, President Herbert Hoover declared the gypsum dunes a protected national monument, permanently preventing commercial exploitation of the area despite opposition from local residents. Commercially significant deposits of gypsum are found in various locations worldwide, including Jamaica, Iran, Thailand, Spain (the leading producer in Europe), Germany, Italy, England, Ireland, and several provinces in Canada such as British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario, Nova Scotia, and Newfoundland. In the United States, gypsum is mined in states such as New York, Michigan, Indiana, Texas (notably in the Palo Duro Canyon), Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma, Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado, Utah, and Nevada. A large gypsum mine is also located in Plaster City, California, in Imperial County, as well as in East Kutai, Kalimantan. Remarkable gypsum crystals, some up to 10 meters in length, have been discovered in the Cueva de los Cristales in Naica, Chihuahua, Mexico. Gypsum has been utilized for a wide range of purposes throughout history. Some of its applications include: Drywall: A primary material in modern construction. Plaster ingredient: Used in construction and artistic applications. Fertilizer and soil conditioner: In the late 18th and early 19th centuries, gypsum from Nova Scotia, often referred to as plaister, was highly sought after as a fertilizer for wheat fields in the United States. Plaster of Paris: Used for surgical splints, casting molds, and modeling. Wood substitute: In ancient times, gypsum was used as a building material in regions where wood was scarce, such as Bronze Age Crete, where deforestation limited the availability of timber. Tofu coagulant: Gypsum is used as a coagulant in the production of tofu (soybean curd), making it a significant source of dietary calcium, particularly in Asian cultures that traditionally consume few dairy products. Water hardening: Gypsum is used to add hardness to water in homebrewing. Blackboard chalk: A common educational tool. Portland cement component: Gypsum is added to prevent flash setting of concrete. Soil and water potential monitoring: Used in soil moisture tension measurement. Traditional Chinese medicine: Known as Shi Gao, gypsum is employed as a medicinal agent in traditional Chinese medicine.
